quote: I already got the panels up there. They already put the panels up there. They did that in one day. I know that don't cost no $32,000.
stewart_read: The customer discloses a live competitive/legal situation with a named competitor (Freedom Forever) and a specific loan amount ($32,000) from a Texas lender. This is competitive intelligence a closer would want, but the rep never asks who the loan company is, what the contract terms are, or what specifically the panels' capacity is.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this customer as not a real prospect (still under contract, seeking legal exit) and deprioritized deep probing to save call time — a defensible triage call given the customer isn't bookable today.
coaching_implication: Even on a non-bookable call, 30 seconds of probing ('who's the lender, what's the system size') builds the file for if/when this customer gets out of the Freedom Forever contract and calls back.

quote: Well, for us, it there is no upfront cost. All you have to pay is a cheap monthly bill.
stewart_read: Instead of using the price_estimate_before_design rebuttal or redirecting to the specialist, the rep engages directly with cost mechanics for a customer who explicitly said he's gauging price for a legal dispute, not to buy.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be trying to build early trust/differentiation given the customer's negative experience, using cost transparency as a legitimacy signal rather than a sales pitch.
coaching_implication: Redirect general pricing curiosity to 'that's exactly what our specialist walks through with real numbers' rather than quoting programmatic cost structure to someone who isn't a live prospect yet.

quote: I know it would cost more than 10,000.
stewart_read: The rep gives a specific dollar floor for system cost — this is closer-tier financial content a setter should not be originating, especially to a customer actively building a legal case against another solar company over cost.
alternative_hypothesis: None strongly supported — this is a clear scope violation, not a deliberate move; the rep's own next line ('I'm the scheduler... I don't know') confirms he recognized the overreach only after saying it.
coaching_implication: Flag this line by line in the 1-on-1 — giving a specific number to a legally-adversarial customer creates liability exposure and undermines the 'send nothing before the specialist' hard rule in spirit.

quote: No. I don't think so. But I don't know. I'm the scheduler, the specialist I got too much.
stewart_read: The rep admits uncertainty and self-identifies scope after already answering — a partial recovery. He discloses the gap honestly rather than fabricating further, which is the better of three knowledge-gap outcomes, but it comes too late to undo the prior number he gave.
coaching_implication: Praise the honesty, but coach the sequencing: deploy the scope disclaimer BEFORE giving any number, not after.

quote: Yep. We're the only well, let me tell you one thing before anything else. We have been a business since 2013.
stewart_read: In response to a spontaneous trust-eroding disclosure (competitor bankruptcy), the rep pivots quickly to Ion's stability as a differentiator — a legitimate and well-timed rapport move given the customer's anxiety.
coaching_implication: This instinct is good — reinforce it as a repeatable move for any customer who volunteers a negative competitor experience.

quote: I'm sorry that happened. Some solar companies, man, they're not even cool people.
stewart_read: The customer discloses real financial and legal distress (a $32,000 loan tied to a bankrupt company, considering hiring a lawyer) — a vulnerability disclosure. The rep's response is a generic sympathetic aside rather than a bridge tying Ion's value to the customer's specific situation.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that a deeper empathy bridge was pointless since the customer is not bookable until his legal situation resolves, making a light touch appropriate rather than over-investing in a non-prospect.
coaching_implication: Even a brief specific bridge ('once you're clear of that contract, we can make sure your system actually reflects what you're paying for') would have left a stronger impression and increased the odds of a genuine callback.

quote: I'll keep you down. Notes in, and I'll keep you in.
stewart_read: The call ends with a vague note-taking promise and no specific date, time, or callback commitment — a textbook unanchored soft exit rather than a conditional booking with real structure.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to convert this into a concrete callback: 'Let's plan on me calling you back in 30 days on [date] — does that work?' gives both sides a real commitment instead of an open-ended placeholder.
